originality.rationale: Arvind et al. define refinability but do not classify its minimal connected-interval failure; Kiefer et al. study cross-graph identification; Cameron et al. give interval recognition; Hanlon/OEIS count graph types without testing orbits. Existing accessible historical claims already name the same eight-vertex double-broom line-graph exception and classify that restricted family, but do not imply uniqueness among all connected interval graphs on up to eight vertices. The novelty here is the *whole interval-class* uniqueness/cutoff, not the pre-existing counterexample. Specialized earlier full coverage remains a residual priority risk.
residual_risks: A specialized prior enumeration of non-refinable interval graphs may already cover the unique eight-vertex failure; none identified by the available searches.

The original Hanlon 1982 enumeration full text was not read; public OEIS count table alone cannot rule out all auxiliary interval-refinement discussion.

value.rationale: This is a sharp, natural complete cutoff in the standard connected interval graph class, a boundary between reliable orbit recovery and its first failure. It proves uniqueness across all 1328 order-eight isomorphism types, rather than recomputing an already-known special-family counterexample. The structural witness supplies an interpretable reason for failure: ordinary degree-equitable counting merges internal path vertices with triangle vertices despite different automorphism orbits. The exact finite fact is motivated independently by the graph family and symmetry invariant and requires a complete exhaustive classification, not a routine direct substitution.
